title: DSA Cold Recall
intro: One card per problem: the state you carry, the invariant that makes it correct, at most two approaches with complexity, one line on why the winner wins, and only the code worth holding in memory. Built from 00-dsa-problem-solving-index.md — 40 patterns, 169 problems.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.state: l at head, r at tail; both skip non-alphanumerics.
problems.invariant: Everything outside [l, r] has already been matched pairwise — the answer depends only on the window still open.

approaches.text: Build a cleaned lowercase copy, compare with its reverse.
Converge in place, skipping junk chars on the fly.

problems.why: The cleaned string is never needed as a value — only the comparison is.

problems.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
problems.state: l, r; sum = a[l] + a[r].
problems.invariant: Array is sorted, so sum too small ⇒ l must rise; too big ⇒ r must fall. Each move kills a whole row or column of pairs.

approaches.text: For each i, binary search the complement.
Converge from both ends.

problems.why: One pointer move discards n candidates at once instead of log-searching for one.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.state: Sorted array; fixed i, then l = i+1, r = n-1.
problems.invariant: After sorting, the inner search is Two Sum II on target -a[i]; duplicates are skipped only at the position where they first appear.

approaches.text: Hash set per pair, dedupe triples in a set.
Sort, fix one, converge on the rest.

problems.why: Sorting makes duplicate-skipping a local check, so no dedupe set is needed.

problems.title: Container With Most Water
problems.state: l, r, best. Area = (r-l) * min(h[l], h[r]).
problems.invariant: Width only shrinks, so the shorter wall caps every future pair it belongs to — once measured it can be discarded.

approaches.text: Converge, always moving the shorter wall inward.

problems.why: Moving the taller wall can never beat the current area — that branch is provably dead.

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
problems.state: l, r, leftMax, rightMax, total.
problems.invariant: If leftMax < rightMax, water above l is fixed at leftMax - h[l] — some wall ≥ leftMax is guaranteed to exist on the right.

approaches.text: Prefix-max and suffix-max arrays, then min(pre, suf) - h[i].
Two pointers carrying the two running maxima.

problems.why: The smaller of the two maxima is already the binding constraint, so the other array is never read.
problems.code:
def trap(height):
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max = right_max = total = 0
    while l < r:
        if height[l] < height[r]:      # left side is bounded by left_max
            left_max = max(left_max, height[l])
            total += left_max - height[l]
            l += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[r])
            total += right_max - height[r]
            r -= 1
    return total

problems.title: Linked List Cycle
problems.state: slow +1 node/tick, fast +2 nodes/tick.
problems.invariant: Inside a cycle of length L the gap closes by exactly 1 each tick, so they must meet within L steps.

approaches.text: HashSet of visited nodes.
Floyd's tortoise and hare.

problems.why: The closing gap replaces the visited set entirely.

problems.title: Happy Number
problems.state: slow = f(n), fast = f(f(n)) where f = digit-square-sum.
problems.invariant: f is a function on a finite set ⇒ every start eventually cycles; the only fixed point is 1.

approaches.text: HashSet of seen sums.
Floyd cycle detection on f.

problems.why: Same termination guarantee, two cursors instead of a growing set.

problems.title: Find the Duplicate Number
problems.state: Read a[i] as a pointer i → a[i]. Phase 1 finds the meet, phase 2 resets one cursor to index 0.
problems.invariant: n+1 slots holding values in [1,n] ⇒ the functional graph must contain a cycle, and its entry node is exactly the duplicated value.

approaches.text: Sort, or a counting array.
Floyd, two phases.

problems.why: Read-only input with O(1) space is the actual constraint, and only the cycle-entry trick satisfies both.

problems.title: Permutation in String
problems.state: count[26] difference array + a matched counter; window length pinned to len(s1).
problems.invariant: Window is a permutation iff all 26 counts agree; only two letters change per slide, so only two counts can flip.

approaches.text: Re-compare all 26 counts on every slide.
Maintain a matched counter, updated on the two changed letters.

problems.why: A slide is a local edit, so the check should be local too.

problems.title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
problems.state: Word length w, total L = w*k. Run w independent word-level windows, one per start offset.
problems.invariant: Any valid start index is congruent to some offset mod w, so w windows cover every possible start.

approaches.text: Check every index by re-counting k words.
w sliding windows over word buckets; shrink on excess or invalid word.

problems.why: Aligning by offset lets the window slide a whole word at a time instead of restarting.
problems.code:
from collections import Counter

def find_substring(s, words):
    w, k = len(words[0]), len(words)
    need = Counter(words)
    res = []
    for offset in range(w):            # w independent word-aligned windows
        l, count, seen = offset, 0, Counter()
        for r in range(offset, len(s) - w + 1, w):
            word = s[r:r + w]
            if word not in need:
                l, count, seen = r + w, 0, Counter()
                continue
            seen[word] += 1
            count += 1
            while seen[word] > need[word]:
                seen[s[l:l + w]] -= 1
                count -= 1
                l += w
            if count == k:
                res.append(l)
                seen[s[l:l + w]] -= 1
                count -= 1
                l += w
    return res

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.state: l, map last[char] → index, best.
problems.invariant: Window [l, r] is always duplicate-free, and l never moves backwards.

approaches.text: Shrink l one step at a time, removing from a set.
Jump l = max(l, last[c] + 1).

problems.why: The last-seen index says exactly where to land, so no per-character shrinking loop is needed.

problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problems.state: l, count[26], maxCount (never decreased), best.
problems.invariant: Window is valid while len - maxCount <= k. A stale-high maxCount only blocks growth — it can never produce a larger wrong answer.

approaches.text: Recompute the window's max count on every step.
Carry a monotonically non-decreasing maxCount.

problems.why: The window only ever grows when a record is broken, so the stale max is harmless.
problems.code:
def character_replacement(s, k):
    count = [0] * 26
    l = max_count = best = 0
    for r, c in enumerate(s):
        count[ord(c) - 65] += 1
        max_count = max(max_count, count[ord(c) - 65])  # never decreased
        if (r - l + 1) - max_count > k:
            count[ord(s[l]) - 65] -= 1
            l += 1                     # window slides, never shrinks
        best = max(best, r - l + 1)
    return best
traps: Never shrink maxCount. Also note the window here never shrinks — it slides.

problems.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
problems.state: l, running sum, best.
problems.invariant: All values are positive ⇒ sum is monotone in window length, so greedy shrinking is safe.

approaches.text: Prefix sums + binary search for each right end.
Shrink-while-valid sliding window.

problems.why: Positivity gives monotonicity, so the left pointer never needs to back up.
problems.code:
def min_sub_array_len(target, nums):
    l = total = 0
    best = float('inf')
    for r, x in enumerate(nums):
        total += x
        while total >= target:         # shrink while still valid
            best = min(best, r - l + 1)
            total -= nums[l]
            l += 1
    return 0 if best == float('inf') else best

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring
problems.state: need[], have[], a formed counter, l, and the best (start, len).
problems.invariant: Window is feasible iff formed == distinct(t). Feasibility is monotone in growth, so one expand/contract sweep sees every candidate minimum.

approaches.text: Test every substring against the count map.
Expand to feasible, then contract while still feasible.

problems.why: Each index enters and leaves the window once, so the sweep is linear rather than quadratic.
problems.code:
from collections import Counter

def min_window(s, t):
    need, have = Counter(t), Counter()
    required, formed = len(need), 0
    l, start, length = 0, 0, float('inf')
    for r, c in enumerate(s):
        have[c] += 1
        if c in need and have[c] == need[c]:
            formed += 1
        while formed == required:      # feasible: record, then contract
            if r - l + 1 < length:
                start, length = l, r - l + 1
            d = s[l]
            have[d] -= 1
            if d in need and have[d] < need[d]:
                formed -= 1
            l += 1
    return "" if length == float('inf') else s[start:start + length]

problems.title: Contains Duplicate II
problems.state: Map value → last index.
problems.invariant: Only the most recent index of a value can satisfy |i - j| <= k, so older ones are safe to overwrite.

approaches.text: Map of last index, overwritten on every visit.

problems.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.state: Running prefix sum, map prefix → count, seeded with {0: 1}.
problems.invariant: Subarray (j, i] sums to k iff pre[i] - pre[j] == k; the map holds counts of every prefix strictly before i.

approaches.text: All O(n²) subarray sums via a running total.
Prefix-count hash map.

problems.why: "Find a matching earlier prefix" collapses into a single hash lookup.
problems.code:
from collections import defaultdict

def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    count = defaultdict(int)
    count[0] = 1                       # empty prefix
    prefix = res = 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        res += count[prefix - k]       # earlier prefixes that leave sum k
        count[prefix] += 1
    return res
traps: Values can be negative, so a sliding window is invalid here. Seeding {0:1} is what counts subarrays starting at index 0.

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.state: Output array used as the prefix pass, then a single running suffix scalar R.
problems.invariant: After pass 1, out[i] is the product of everything left of i; pass 2 multiplies in the running right product.

approaches.text: Separate prefix and suffix arrays.
Two passes, suffix carried in one variable.

problems.why: The right product is only ever needed at one index at a time.
problems.code:
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    for i in range(1, n):              # out[i] = product of nums[:i]
        out[i] = out[i - 1] * nums[i - 1]
    R = 1                              # product of nums[i+1:]
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= R
        R *= nums[i]
    return out

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problems.state: HashSet of all values; walk only from run heads.
problems.invariant: Start a walk at x only when x-1 is absent — that makes every element the member of exactly one walk.

approaches.text: Sort, then scan for runs.
Set + start-only-at-run-heads.

problems.why: The no-predecessor guard is what keeps total walk work linear instead of quadratic.

problems.title: Maximum Subarray
problems.state: cur = best sum ending at i, best = global.
problems.invariant: A prefix with negative sum can never help a later subarray, so it is dropped rather than carried.

approaches.text: Prefix sums with a running minimum prefix.
Kadane.

problems.why: Identical idea in one variable — cur = max(a[i], cur + a[i]).

problems.title: Maximum Product Subarray
problems.state: curMax and curMin — a negative value swaps their roles.
problems.invariant: Best product ending at i is one of a[i], curMax*a[i], curMin*a[i], so the minimum must be tracked too.

approaches.text: Track both extremes, swapping on a negative.

problems.why: A large negative minimum is one multiplication away from being the maximum.

problems.title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
problems.state: Kadane max, Kadane min, and the total sum.
problems.invariant: A wrapping subarray's complement is a non-wrapping one ⇒ best wrap = total - minSubarray.

approaches.text: Duplicate the array and run a length-bounded Kadane.
max(kadaneMax, total - kadaneMin).

problems.why: The complement trick handles wrap-around without materialising 2n elements.
problems.code:
def max_subarray_sum_circular(nums):
    total = cur_max = cur_min = 0
    best_max = best_min = nums[0]
    for x in nums:
        cur_max = max(x, cur_max + x)
        best_max = max(best_max, cur_max)
        cur_min = min(x, cur_min + x)
        best_min = min(best_min, cur_min)
        total += x
    if best_max < 0:                   # all negative: wrapping would be empty
        return best_max
    return max(best_max, total - best_min)
traps: If every element is negative, total - minSum is 0 (the empty subarray) — hence the maxSum > 0 guard.

problems.title: Remove Element
problems.state: Write pointer k.
problems.invariant: [0, k) holds every kept element, in original order.

approaches.text: Read/write two-pointer compaction.

problems.title: Sort Colors
problems.state: low, mid, high.
problems.invariant: [0,low) = 0s, [low,mid) = 1s, (high,n) = 2s, [mid,high] unexamined.

approaches.text: Counting sort in two passes.
One-pass Dutch National Flag partition.

problems.why: Single pass, and it generalises to keys you cannot count.
traps: On the 2-swap you do NOT advance mid — the value swapped in from high is still unexamined.

problems.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
problems.state: Write pointer k; compare against a[k-2].
problems.invariant: Keep a[i] iff k < 2 or a[i] != a[k-2] — that bounds every value to two copies in [0,k).

approaches.text: Write pointer with a look-back of 2.

problems.why: Generalises to "keep at most m" by comparing against a[k-m].
problems.code:
def remove_duplicates(nums):
    k = 0                              # write pointer
    for x in nums:
        if k < 2 or x != nums[k - 2]:  # at most two copies
            nums[k] = x
            k += 1
    return k

problems.title: Summary Ranges
problems.state: Run start index.
problems.invariant: A run breaks exactly where a[i] + 1 != a[i+1].

approaches.text: Single scan, extending the current run.

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.state: Sorted by start; the last merged interval sits on the output tail.
problems.invariant: After sorting by start, an interval can only overlap the current tail — never an earlier one.

approaches.text: Repeatedly scan for any overlapping pair and merge.
Sort by start, one pass extending the tail.

problems.why: Sorting reduces overlap from a global search to one local comparison.

problems.title: Insert Interval
problems.state: Three phases — strictly before, overlapping, strictly after.
problems.invariant: Input is already sorted and disjoint ⇒ the set of intervals overlapping the new one is one contiguous block.

approaches.text: Three-phase linear scan, no sort needed.

problems.why: The pre-existing sort is the whole reason this is O(n) and not O(n log n).
problems.code:
def insert(intervals, new_interval):
    res, i, n = [], 0, len(intervals)
    start, end = new_interval
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < start:     # 1. strictly before
        res.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= end:      # 2. overlapping: absorb
        start = min(start, intervals[i][0])
        end = max(end, intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    res.append([start, end])
    res.extend(intervals[i:])                    # 3. strictly after
    return res

problems.title: Missing Number
problems.state: One accumulator XOR-ing every index and every value.
problems.invariant: Values are a permutation of [0,n] with one removed ⇒ XOR-ing indices against values cancels all pairs, leaving the missing one.

approaches.text: Sum formula n(n+1)/2 − sum.
XOR of all indices and all values.

problems.why: XOR is overflow-proof and needs no closed form.

problems.title: First Missing Positive
problems.state: Place value v into slot v-1 by swapping.
problems.invariant: After the placement pass, a[i] == i+1 for every value present in [1,n]; the first index violating that is the answer.

approaches.text: Hash set of values, then probe 1..n+1.
Cyclic sort in place.

problems.why: The array itself is the hash table — index i is the natural bucket for value i+1.
traps: Loop condition is a[a[i]-1] != a[i], not a[i] != i+1 — otherwise duplicates spin forever.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms
problems.state: Sorted by start; previous end.
problems.invariant: Once sorted by start, a conflict can only be with the immediately previous meeting.

approaches.text: Sort by start, compare adjacent pairs.

problems.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
problems.state: Sort by end; keep prevEnd and a kept count.
problems.invariant: Among conflicting intervals, keeping the one that finishes earliest leaves the most room for everything after — the exchange argument.

approaches.text: DP on the longest non-conflicting chain.
Sort by end, greedily keep.

problems.why: Earliest-finish-time is provably optimal, so no DP table is needed.
traps: Sorting by start instead of end silently gives wrong answers on nested intervals.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
problems.state: Sort by end; arrow position = the current interval's end.
problems.invariant: Same exchange argument — shoot at the earliest end, and it bursts every balloon that starts before it.

approaches.text: Sort by end, fire a new arrow only on a true miss.

problems.why: Identical to Non-overlapping Intervals with the answer read off the other way.
problems.code:
def find_min_arrow_shots(points):
    points.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])
    arrows, arrow = 0, float('-inf')
    for start, end in points:
        if start > arrow:              # true miss: fire at this balloon's end
            arrows += 1
            arrow = end
    return arrows
traps: Touching endpoints count as overlap here, so the test is > and not >=.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms II
problems.state: Min-heap of end times; sorted by start.
problems.invariant: Heap size = rooms currently occupied; only the earliest-ending room can possibly be freed by the next meeting.

approaches.text: Sweep line: sort starts and ends separately, +1/−1.
Min-heap of end times.

problems.why: The heap answers "is any room free" in O(log n) and directly models room reuse.

problems.title: IPO
problems.state: Min-heap by capital (locked projects), max-heap by profit (affordable projects), running capital w.
problems.invariant: Every project with capital <= w has already been moved into the profit heap, so the greedy pick is always its top.

approaches.text: Two heaps: unlock by capital, pick by profit.

problems.why: Affordability only ever grows, so a project moves between heaps exactly once.

problems.title: Find Median from Data Stream
problems.state: Max-heap lo (smaller half), min-heap hi (larger half).
problems.invariant: Every element of lo ≤ every element of hi, and size(lo) equals size(hi) or exceeds it by one.

approaches.text: Sorted list with binary-search insertion.
Two balanced heaps.

problems.why: Only the boundary between the two halves matters, and heaps expose exactly that.
traps: Always push through lo first — pushing directly into hi breaks the ordering invariant.

problems.title: Binary Search
problems.state: lo, hi inclusive; mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2.
problems.invariant: If the target exists it lies in [lo, hi]; the loop runs while lo <= hi.

approaches.text: Classic inclusive-bounds binary search.

problems.title: Search a 2D Matrix
problems.state: One index over the flattened matrix; (mid / n, mid % n).
problems.invariant: Rows are sorted and each row's first element exceeds the previous row's last ⇒ the matrix is one sorted array of length m·n.

approaches.text: Binary search the row, then binary search inside it.
Single binary search over m·n.

problems.why: Same complexity, one loop, and no boundary bugs between two searches.

problems.title: Find Peak Element
problems.state: lo, hi; compare a[mid] with a[mid+1].
problems.invariant: Neighbours always differ and the edges act as −∞, so whichever half you keep is guaranteed to contain a peak.

approaches.text: Binary search on the slope direction.

problems.why: You are searching a shape, not a value — the slope tells you which half must contain a peak.

problems.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
problems.state: Two lower-bound searches.
problems.invariant: lowerBound(t) = first index with a[i] >= t; the last position is lowerBound(t+1) - 1.

approaches.text: Two lower-bound calls.

problems.why: Writing one clean lowerBound and calling it twice removes the usual off-by-one mess.

problems.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.state: lo, hi; compare a[mid] against a[hi].
problems.invariant: a[mid] > a[hi] ⇒ the pivot is strictly right of mid; otherwise the minimum is at mid or to its left.

approaches.text: Binary search comparing mid to the right endpoint.

traps: Compare to a[hi], never a[lo] — comparing to lo breaks on an unrotated array.

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.state: lo, hi; at every step one half is fully sorted.
problems.invariant: a[lo] <= a[mid] means the left half is sorted — then check whether the target lies inside that sorted range.

approaches.text: Find the pivot, then binary search the correct segment.
One pass, deciding which half is sorted.

problems.why: The sorted half is decidable from three values, so the pivot pass is redundant.

problems.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.state: Binary search the cut i in the shorter array; j = (m+n+1)/2 - i.
problems.invariant: A valid partition satisfies A[i-1] <= B[j] and B[j-1] <= A[i]; the left side then holds exactly half the elements.

approaches.text: Merge until you reach the middle.
Binary search the partition on the shorter array.

problems.why: The median depends only on the four values straddling the cut, never on the full merge.
traps: Use ±infinity for out-of-range i and j, and always binary search the shorter array so j stays in bounds.

problems.title: Sqrt(x)
problems.state: lo = 0, hi = x; find the largest m with m*m <= x.
problems.invariant: The predicate m*m <= x is monotone true→false, so you keep the last true.

approaches.text: Binary search the answer, keeping the last feasible value.

traps: Use m <= x/m rather than m*m <= x to dodge overflow.

problems.title: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.state: lo = 1, hi = max(pile); feasible(k) = Σ ceil(p/k) <= h.
problems.invariant: Feasibility is monotone in k — a faster speed is never worse — which is the entire licence to binary search a value that is not in the array.

approaches.text: Try every speed from 1 upward.
Binary search the answer space.

problems.why: Monotone feasibility turns a linear scan of candidate answers into a logarithmic one.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.state: Frequency map, then buckets indexed by frequency.
problems.invariant: Frequency is bounded by n ⇒ it is a valid array index; walking buckets from n down to 1 yields descending frequency.

approaches.text: Frequency map + min-heap of size k.
Bucket sort by frequency.

problems.why: The frequency range is bounded by n, so counting beats comparing.

problems.title: K Closest Points to Origin
problems.state: Max-heap of size k, ordered by squared distance.
problems.invariant: The heap always holds the k best seen so far, and its root is the worst of those k.

approaches.text: Sort everything by distance.
Bounded max-heap (or quickselect for O(n) average).

problems.why: You never need the other n−k points in any order.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problems.state: Quickselect with a random pivot; target index n-k.
problems.invariant: After a partition the pivot sits at its final sorted index, so only one side can contain the target.

approaches.text: Min-heap of size k.
Quickselect with a randomised pivot.

problems.why: Half the remaining work is discarded each round instead of being ordered.
traps: Without a random (or median-of-three) pivot, sorted input degrades this to O(n²).

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.state: f = max frequency, c = how many tasks tie at f.
problems.invariant: The busiest task lays out f-1 full frames of size n+1; every other task simply fills those idle slots.

approaches.text: Greedy simulation with a max-heap and a cooldown queue.
Closed form: max(len, (f-1)(n+1) + c).

problems.why: The schedule length is entirely determined by the busiest task — simulation only re-derives the formula.
traps: The max(...) with tasks.length is what handles the case where there are too many distinct tasks to ever idle.

problems.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
problems.state: Dummy head + tail pointer.
problems.invariant: tail always points at the last node of the built list; both inputs remain sorted ahead of their cursors.

approaches.text: Dummy-head splice merge.

problems.why: The dummy head removes every "is this the first node" special case.

problems.title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
problems.state: Min-heap seeded with (i, 0) for the first k rows; pop (i,j), push (i, j+1).
problems.invariant: Sums increase along each row, so only one candidate per row can ever be the next smallest — the heap holds that frontier.

approaches.text: Build all m·n sums and sort.
Heap over per-row frontiers.

problems.why: Row-wise monotonicity means the next answer is always already in the heap.
problems.code:
import heapq

def k_smallest_pairs(nums1, nums2, k):
    heap = [(nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0) for i in range(min(k, len(nums1)))]
    heapq.heapify(heap)                # one frontier per row i
    res = []
    while heap and len(res) < k:
        _, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        res.append([nums1[i], nums2[j]])
        if j + 1 < len(nums2):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (nums1[i] + nums2[j + 1], i, j + 1))
    return res

problems.title: Merge k Sorted Lists
problems.state: Pairwise merge rounds with a doubling interval (or a min-heap of the k heads).
problems.invariant: Each merge round halves the number of lists, so every node is copied exactly log k times.

approaches.text: Min-heap of the k current heads.
Divide and conquer pairwise merge.

problems.why: Same time bound with no heap — each round is just the two-list merge you already know.

problems.title: Daily Temperatures
problems.state: Stack of indices with strictly decreasing temperatures.
problems.invariant: Anything on the stack is still waiting for a warmer day; a new warmer day resolves all of them at once.

approaches.text: For each day, scan forward.
Decreasing monotonic stack of indices.

problems.why: Each index is pushed and popped exactly once, so the total scan is linear.
traps: Push indices, not temperatures — you need the distance.

problems.title: Car Fleet
problems.state: Sort by position descending; stack of fleet arrival times.
problems.invariant: A car merges into the fleet ahead iff its arrival time ≤ that fleet's; the stack top is always the slowest fleet ahead.

approaches.text: Sort descending by position, push only strictly slower cars.

problems.why: You can drop the stack entirely and just carry the max arrival time seen so far.

problems.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
problems.state: Stack of indices with increasing heights; a sentinel 0 appended at the end.
problems.invariant: For a popped bar, the incoming index is its right boundary and the element beneath it on the stack is its left boundary — both become known at exactly the pop moment.

approaches.text: For each bar, expand left and right.
Increasing monotonic stack, area computed on pop.

problems.why: The pop moment is precisely when both boundaries of that bar are determined.
problems.code:
def largest_rectangle_area(heights):
    stack, best = [], 0                # indices, heights increasing
    for i, h in enumerate(heights + [0]):      # sentinel 0 flushes the stack
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= h:
            height = heights[stack.pop()]
            left = stack[-1] if stack else -1
            best = max(best, height * (i - left - 1))
        stack.append(i)
    return best
traps: Width is i - st.peek() - 1 AFTER the pop, not i - poppedIndex.

problems.title: Sliding Window Maximum
problems.state: Deque of indices whose values decrease front → back.
problems.invariant: The front is the window max; any index holding a value ≤ the incoming one can never be a maximum again.

approaches.text: Max-heap with lazy deletion.
Decreasing monotonic deque.

problems.why: An earlier, smaller element is dominated forever — so it is deleted, not merely deprioritised.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.state: Stack of expected closing brackets.
problems.invariant: The stack holds unclosed openers in the exact order they must be closed.

approaches.text: Push the matching closer, pop and compare.

problems.why: Pushing the closer rather than the opener removes the pair-lookup at pop time.

problems.title: Min Stack
problems.state: Main stack storing (value, minSoFar) pairs.
problems.invariant: The minimum at each depth is fixed at push time and can never change while that element is on the stack.

approaches.text: A second stack mirroring every push.
Store the running min alongside the value.

problems.why: The min is a property of the stack depth, so it belongs in the frame.

problems.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
problems.state: Operand stack.
problems.invariant: RPN guarantees both operands are already on the stack when an operator arrives — and the second pop is the left operand.

approaches.text: Single pass with an operand stack.

problems.title: Basic Calculator
problems.state: Running res, current sign, stack alternating (resultBeforeParen, signBeforeParen).
problems.invariant: '(' saves the outer context and resets; ')' folds the inner result back in with the saved sign.

approaches.text: Convert to postfix, then evaluate.
Single pass with a sign stack.

problems.why: With only + and −, the paren context is just two integers, so no postfix conversion is needed.

problems.title: Reverse Linked List
problems.state: prev, cur, next.
problems.invariant: prev heads the already-reversed prefix; cur heads the untouched suffix.

approaches.text: Three-pointer iterative reversal.

problems.why: Recursion is O(n) stack for no gain — the iterative form is the one to have in muscle memory.
problems.code:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    return prev

problems.title: Reverse Linked List II
problems.state: Dummy head; before = node at position left-1; then head-insertion.
problems.invariant: After k insertions the sublist [left, left+k] is reversed and still correctly spliced at both ends.

approaches.text: Head-insertion of the following nodes, one pass.

problems.why: Head-insertion avoids having to re-find and re-attach the two boundary nodes afterwards.
problems.code:
def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    before = dummy
    for _ in range(left - 1):
        before = before.next           # node at position left-1
    cur = before.next                  # becomes the tail of the reversed part
    for _ in range(right - left):
        move = cur.next                # head-insert the node after cur
        cur.next = move.next
        move.next = before.next
        before.next = move
    return dummy.next

problems.title: Reorder List
problems.state: Three phases — find the middle (fast/slow), reverse the second half, then interleave.
problems.invariant: After splitting, the halves differ in length by at most one, so the weave terminates cleanly with the first half ending the list.

approaches.text: Split, reverse, weave.

problems.why: It is three routines you already own, composed — nothing new to memorise.
problems.code:
def reorder_list(head):
    slow, fast = head, head.next       # 1. find the middle
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
    second, slow.next = slow.next, None

    prev = None                        # 2. reverse the second half
    while second:
        nxt = second.next
        second.next = prev
        prev, second = second, nxt

    first, second = head, prev         # 3. weave
    while second:
        n1, n2 = first.next, second.next
        first.next = second
        second.next = n1
        first, second = n1, n2

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
problems.state: Dummy head; fast advanced n+1 steps, then both move together.
problems.invariant: The gap between fast and slow is pinned at n+1, so when fast falls off the end, slow is the predecessor of the target.

approaches.text: Count the length, then walk to len − n.
Fixed-gap two pointers with a dummy head.

problems.why: The fixed gap encodes "n from the end" without ever knowing the length.
traps: The dummy head is what makes deleting the first node work without a branch.

problems.title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
problems.state: groupPrev; check k nodes exist, reverse that block, relink both ends.
problems.invariant: groupPrev always points at the last node of the finished output; a trailing partial group is left untouched.

approaches.text: Verify k nodes, reverse in place, advance groupPrev.

problems.why: The "look ahead k nodes first" check is the only thing separating this from plain reversal.
problems.code:
def reverse_k_group(head, k):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    group_prev = dummy
    while True:
        kth = group_prev               # 1. check that k nodes exist
        for _ in range(k):
            kth = kth.next
            if not kth:
                return dummy.next
        group_next = kth.next

        prev, cur = group_next, group_prev.next   # 2. reverse the block
        while cur is not group_next:
            nxt = cur.next
            cur.next = prev
            prev, cur = cur, nxt

        first = group_prev.next        # 3. relink; old first is the new tail
        group_prev.next = kth
        group_prev = first

problems.title: Average of Levels in Binary Tree
problems.state: Queue + a level-size snapshot taken at the top of each iteration.
problems.invariant: Taking exactly queue.size() nodes at the start of an iteration isolates one complete level.

approaches.text: BFS with a level-size loop.

problems.why: Snapshotting the size before the inner loop is the entire level-order idiom.

problems.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
problems.state: Same queue + level-size snapshot.
problems.invariant: The queue holds exactly one full level at the top of each outer iteration.

approaches.text: BFS with a level-size loop.

problems.title: Binary Tree Right Side View
problems.state: Level loop; take the last node dequeued in each level.
problems.invariant: Children are enqueued left then right, so the last node of a level is its rightmost.

approaches.text: DFS root→right→left, recording the first visit per depth.
BFS taking each level's last node.

problems.why: Same cost, but BFS makes "rightmost at this depth" literal instead of an ordering trick.

problems.title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
problems.state: Level loop + a direction flag; per-level deque.
problems.invariant: Traversal order never changes — only the insertion end of the per-level list flips.

approaches.text: BFS with an alternating insertion end.

problems.why: Flipping insertion beats reversing the queue, which would break the child ordering.

problems.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problems.state: Recursion returning depth.
problems.invariant: depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(children)); a null node has depth 0.

approaches.text: Post-order recursion.

problems.title: Same Tree
problems.state: Parallel recursion over both trees.
problems.invariant: Two trees are equal iff the roots match and both subtree pairs match — structure and value checked in the same call.

approaches.text: Simultaneous post-order comparison.

problems.title: Invert Binary Tree
problems.state: Swap children, recurse.
problems.invariant: Swapping once at every node produces the mirror; swap-before or swap-after recursion are equivalent.

approaches.text: Recursive swap at every node.

problems.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
problems.state: DFS returns height; a global best holds the through-node path length.
problems.invariant: The diameter passes through exactly one highest node — where it equals leftHeight + rightHeight.

approaches.text: Compute both heights separately at every node.
Single post-order returning height, updating a global.

problems.why: The return value and the answer are different quantities — that split is the whole pattern.

problems.title: Balanced Binary Tree
problems.state: DFS returns height, or -1 as an "unbalanced" sentinel.
problems.invariant: The sentinel propagates upward, so the first imbalance short-circuits the entire remaining tree.

approaches.text: Check the height gap at every node with a separate height call.
Post-order with a −1 sentinel.

problems.why: Heights are computed once and reused on the way up instead of recomputed on the way down.

problems.title: Subtree of Another Tree
problems.state: Serialise both trees with explicit null markers, then substring-search.
problems.invariant: Null markers make the preorder serialisation unambiguous, so subtree containment becomes substring containment.

approaches.text: Run sameTree at every node of s.
Serialise with null markers + string search.

problems.why: One unambiguous encoding replaces n separate structural comparisons.
traps: Without the separator, values 2 and 12 collide — the comma is load-bearing.

problems.title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
problems.state: Preorder cursor + inorder value → index map + (lo, hi) bounds.
problems.invariant: Preorder hands you the next root; that root's inorder index splits the remaining range into left and right subtrees.

approaches.text: Linear scan of inorder to find each root.
Index map + range recursion.

problems.why: The split point becomes a lookup instead of a scan.
problems.code:
def build_tree(preorder, inorder):
    index = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(inorder)}
    pre = 0                            # next root in preorder

    def build(lo, hi):                 # subtree over inorder[lo..hi]
        nonlocal pre
        if lo > hi:
            return None
        root = TreeNode(preorder[pre])
        pre += 1
        mid = index[root.val]
        root.left = build(lo, mid - 1)     # left first: preorder order
        root.right = build(mid + 1, hi)
        return root

    return build(0, len(inorder) - 1)
traps: Build left before right — the shared preorder cursor makes the order load-bearing.

problems.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
problems.state: DFS returns the best downward chain (clamped at 0); a global holds the through-node best.
problems.invariant: A parent can only use one of a node's two branches, so the returned value is deliberately different from the answer recorded at that node.

approaches.text: Post-order with a clamped return and a global max.

problems.why: Clamping negatives to 0 is how "don't take this branch" is expressed without a branch.
problems.code:
def max_path_sum(root):
    best = float('-inf')

    def gain(node):                    # best downward chain from node
        nonlocal best
        if not node:
            return 0
        l = max(gain(node.left), 0)    # clamp: drop negative branches
        r = max(gain(node.right), 0)
        best = max(best, node.val + l + r)
        return node.val + max(l, r)

    gain(root)
    return best

problems.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
problems.state: Preorder with # for nulls; a single cursor on decode.
problems.invariant: Null markers make the preorder sequence uniquely reconstructible, so no second traversal is needed.

approaches.text: Level-order with null placeholders.
Preorder with # markers, recursive rebuild.

problems.why: Decode is the same recursion as encode, so one cursor reconstructs the tree.

problems.title: Minimum Absolute Difference in BST
problems.state: In-order traversal + prev value.
problems.invariant: In-order of a BST is sorted, so the minimum gap must be between two adjacent visits.

approaches.text: In-order traversal tracking the previous value.

problems.code:
def get_minimum_difference(root):
    best, prev = float('inf'), None

    def inorder(node):                 # BST in-order = sorted
        nonlocal best, prev
        if not node:
            return
        inorder(node.left)
        if prev is not None:
            best = min(best, node.val - prev)
        prev = node.val
        inorder(node.right)

    inorder(root)
    return best

problems.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problems.state: (lo, hi) bounds passed down the recursion.
problems.invariant: Every node must lie strictly inside the bounds inherited from all its ancestors — not merely beat its parent.

approaches.text: In-order traversal, check strictly increasing.
Bounds recursion.

problems.why: Bounds make the grandparent-violation case impossible to forget.
traps: Use long (or nullable) bounds — Integer.MIN_VALUE appears as a legal node value.

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
problems.state: Iterative in-order with an explicit stack and a counter.
problems.invariant: In-order visits values in ascending order, so the k-th pop is the answer.

approaches.text: Full in-order into a list, then index k−1.
Iterative in-order, stop at the k-th pop.

problems.why: It stops early — you never traverse past the answer.
problems.code:
def kth_smallest(root, k):
    stack, node = [], root
    while True:
        while node:                    # push the left spine
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:
            return node.val
        node = node.right

problems.title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
problems.state: Stack holding the current left spine.
problems.invariant: The stack top is always the next smallest; each node is pushed and popped once, giving amortised O(1).

approaches.text: Controlled iterative in-order via a left-spine stack.

problems.why: It is Kth-Smallest with the loop turned inside out into next()/hasNext().

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
problems.state: A single walk down from the root.
problems.invariant: If both targets sit on the same side of node.val, the LCA is on that side; the first split point is the LCA.

approaches.text: Iterative walk using the BST ordering.

problems.why: The ordering means you never have to search the other subtree at all.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
problems.state: Post-order returning "p, q, or the LCA found below".
problems.invariant: A node is the LCA iff both subtree calls return non-null, or it is itself a target with a hit beneath it.

approaches.text: Single post-order returning the found node.

problems.why: Returning the found node instead of a boolean lets one traversal answer both questions.

problems.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
problems.state: children[26] + isEnd per node.
problems.invariant: A root-to-node path spells a prefix; isEnd marks that this prefix is also a complete word.

approaches.text: Array-children trie.

problems.why: isEnd is the only thing separating "a word exists" from "a prefix exists".

problems.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
problems.state: Trie + a DFS that forks on '.'.
problems.invariant: '.' branches into all 26 children at that depth; every other character is a single deterministic step.

approaches.text: Trie with a branching DFS for wildcards.
approaches.complexity: O(L) avg, O(26^d) worst / O(L) stack

problems.why: The wildcard is the only place the walk becomes a search.

problems.title: Word Search II
problems.state: Trie of the whole dictionary + one grid DFS carrying the current trie node.
problems.invariant: The DFS continues only while the path is still a valid trie prefix, so a dead prefix kills every word that shares it.

approaches.text: Run Word Search once per word.
One grid DFS driven by a trie of all words.

problems.why: All words are searched in a single pass, and one prefix miss prunes an entire family.
traps: Null out node.word after collecting it — that is the dedupe, not a HashSet.

problems.title: Rotting Oranges
problems.state: Queue seeded with all rotten cells, a fresh counter, a minute counter.
problems.invariant: Multi-source BFS expands every source in lockstep, so the level index is the elapsed minute.

approaches.text: BFS from each rotten cell separately, take per-cell minimum.
Multi-source BFS, one level = one minute.

problems.why: Seeding all sources at level 0 computes every cell's nearest-source distance in one sweep.

problems.title: Walls and Gates
problems.state: Queue seeded with all gates; distances written into the grid itself.
problems.invariant: The first time BFS reaches a room that distance is minimal, so INF doubles as the visited flag.

approaches.text: Multi-source BFS from every gate.

problems.why: Writing distances in place removes both the visited set and the distance array.

problems.title: Snakes and Ladders
problems.state: Flatten the boustrophedon board to 1..n²; BFS over die rolls.
problems.invariant: Every roll costs 1, so BFS level = minimum number of moves.

approaches.text: BFS over the flattened board.

problems.why: Unweighted edges are exactly the condition that makes BFS optimal — no Dijkstra needed.
traps: The index-to-(row,col) flattening is the whole bug surface: rows count from the bottom and odd rows run right-to-left.

problems.title: Word Ladder
problems.state: BFS over words; neighbours found through wildcard buckets like h*t.
problems.invariant: All edges cost 1 ⇒ BFS depth is the shortest transformation sequence length.

approaches.text: Compare every pair of words to build the edge list.
Wildcard-pattern buckets + BFS.

problems.why: Bucketing by wildcard finds neighbours without any all-pairs comparison.

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.state: Sink in place by overwriting '1' → '0'.
problems.invariant: Each DFS consumes one entire connected component, so the number of launches is the number of islands.

approaches.text: DFS sinking each component on first contact.

problems.why: Overwriting the grid removes the separate visited array.

problems.title: Max Area of Island
problems.state: DFS returning the component size.
problems.invariant: Mark before recursing, so each cell contributes to exactly one area sum.

approaches.text: DFS returning 1 + the four recursive sizes.

problems.title: Clone Graph
problems.state: Map original → clone, used as both memo and visited set.
problems.invariant: A node is cloned exactly once, and the map lookup is precisely what breaks cycles.

approaches.text: DFS with an original→clone map.

problems.why: Registering the clone in the map before recursing is what makes cycles terminate.

problems.title: Surrounded Regions
problems.state: DFS launched only from border 'O's, marking them safe.
problems.invariant: An 'O' survives iff it is connected to the border, so mark the survivors and flip the complement.

approaches.text: DFS each region and check whether it touched the border.
Mark from the border, then flip everything unmarked.

problems.why: Inverting the question removes the per-region "did it escape" flag entirely.

problems.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
problems.state: Two reachability grids; DFS inward from each ocean's border, stepping only to cells of ≥ height.
problems.invariant: Reversing the flow direction turns "can this cell reach the ocean" into "can the ocean reach this cell".

approaches.text: DFS from every cell to test both oceans.
Reverse DFS from both borders, then intersect.

problems.why: Reversing makes each ocean one sweep instead of one sweep per cell.
problems.code:
def pacific_atlantic(heights):
    m, n = len(heights), len(heights[0])

    def reach(starts):                 # walk uphill inward from an ocean
        seen = set(starts)
        stack = list(starts)
        while stack:
            r, c = stack.pop()
            for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                if (0 <= nr < m and 0 <= nc < n and (nr, nc) not in seen
                        and heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]):
                    seen.add((nr, nc))
                    stack.append((nr, nc))
        return seen

    pacific = reach([(0, c) for c in range(n)] + [(r, 0) for r in range(m)])
    atlantic = reach([(m - 1, c) for c in range(n)] + [(r, n - 1) for r in range(m)])
    return [list(cell) for cell in pacific & atlantic]

problems.title: Course Schedule
problems.state: Indegree array + a queue of zero-indegree nodes (Kahn's).
problems.invariant: A DAG always has some node with indegree 0; if fewer than n nodes get processed, a cycle exists.

approaches.text: DFS with white/grey/black colouring to spot a back edge.
Kahn's BFS over indegrees.

problems.why: One counter gives both the cycle check and the ordering, with no recursion state to manage.
problems.code:
from collections import deque

def can_finish(num_courses, prerequisites):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(num_courses)]
    indegree = [0] * num_courses
    for course, pre in prerequisites:
        graph[pre].append(course)
        indegree[course] += 1
    queue = deque(i for i in range(num_courses) if indegree[i] == 0)
    taken = 0
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        taken += 1
        for nxt in graph[node]:
            indegree[nxt] -= 1
            if indegree[nxt] == 0:
                queue.append(nxt)
    return taken == num_courses        # a cycle leaves nodes never freed

problems.title: Course Schedule II
problems.state: Same as above, recording the pop order.
problems.invariant: A node is emitted only after every prerequisite has been, so the pop order is a valid topological order.

approaches.text: Kahn's BFS, collecting the pop order.

problems.code:
from collections import deque

def find_order(num_courses, prerequisites):
    graph = [[] for _ in range(num_courses)]
    indegree = [0] * num_courses
    for course, pre in prerequisites:
        graph[pre].append(course)
        indegree[course] += 1
    queue = deque(i for i in range(num_courses) if indegree[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(node)             # pop order is a valid schedule
        for nxt in graph[node]:
            indegree[nxt] -= 1
            if indegree[nxt] == 0:
                queue.append(nxt)
    return order if len(order) == num_courses else []

problems.state: Edges from the first differing character of each adjacent word pair, then Kahn's.
problems.invariant: Only the first mismatch between two adjacent words carries information; everything after it is unconstrained.

approaches.text: Build edges from adjacent pairs, then topological sort.

problems.why: The reduction to a graph is the whole problem — the sort itself is stock Kahn's.
traps: The prefix-longer-than-its-prefix case is invalid input, not just a missing edge.

problems.title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
problems.state: parent[] + rank; a component counter starting at n.
problems.invariant: Each successful union merges two distinct sets, so that is exactly when the count drops.

approaches.text: DFS or BFS over an adjacency list.
Union-Find with path compression.

problems.why: No adjacency list is needed, and it works when edges arrive as a stream.

problems.title: Graph Valid Tree
problems.state: Union-Find + an edge count check.
problems.invariant: A tree is exactly "n-1 edges AND no cycle" — either condition alone is insufficient.

approaches.text: Edge-count check + union-find cycle detection.

problems.why: The count check rules out forests; the cycle check rules out multi-edges.

problems.title: Redundant Connection
problems.state: Union-Find over edges in input order.
problems.invariant: The first edge whose endpoints already share a root closes the cycle — and since edges are processed in order, that is also the last such edge in the input.

approaches.text: Union-find, return on the first same-root edge.

problems.title: Evaluate Division
problems.state: Weighted union-find: w[x] = x / root(x).
problems.invariant: A query a/b is w[a] / w[b] whenever a and b share a root; otherwise the answer is −1.

approaches.text: Build a weighted graph, DFS per query.
Weighted union-find with weight-aware path compression.

problems.why: Compression folds an entire chain into one ratio, so repeated queries become near-constant.

problems.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
problems.state: Prim's: min-heap of (cost, node) + a visited set.
problems.invariant: MST cut property — the cheapest edge crossing the visited / unvisited boundary is always safe to take.

approaches.text: Kruskal: sort all n² edges, union-find.
Prim's over the implicit complete graph.

problems.why: The graph is complete, so generating edges lazily from the heap beats materialising all n² of them.
problems.code:
import heapq

def min_cost_connect_points(points):
    n = len(points)
    visited = set()
    heap = [(0, 0)]                    # (cost to attach, point)
    total = 0
    while len(visited) < n:
        cost, i = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if i in visited:
            continue
        visited.add(i)
        total += cost
        xi, yi = points[i]
        for j in range(n):
            if j not in visited:
                xj, yj = points[j]
                heapq.heappush(heap, (abs(xi - xj) + abs(yi - yj), j))
    return total

problems.title: Network Delay Time
problems.state: Min-heap of (dist, node) + a finalised set.
problems.invariant: With non-negative weights, the first time a node is popped its distance is final.

approaches.text: Bellman-Ford relaxing all edges V times.
Dijkstra with a min-heap.

problems.why: Non-negative weights let you finalise on pop instead of re-relaxing repeatedly.

problems.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
problems.state: dist[] relaxed exactly k+1 times, each round reading a snapshot of the previous round.
problems.invariant: After round i, dist[v] is the cheapest cost using at most i edges — and the snapshot is what enforces "at most i".

approaches.text: Dijkstra over (cost, node, stops) states.
Bellman-Ford limited to k+1 rounds over a cloned array.

problems.why: The hop limit is literally a round counter here, and Dijkstra's finalise-on-pop is unsound once stops constrain the path.
traps: Forget the clone and one round can chain multiple edges, silently exceeding k stops.

problems.title: Swim in Rising Water
problems.state: Min-heap ordered by cell elevation; the answer is the running max along the chosen path.
problems.invariant: Path cost here is the max along the path, not the sum — so relaxation uses max instead of +.

approaches.text: Binary search the threshold t + BFS over cells ≤ t.
Dijkstra with the relax operator swapped to max.

problems.why: A minimax path is just Dijkstra with + replaced by max — same proof, same finalise-on-pop.

problems.title: Single Number
problems.state: One running XOR accumulator.
problems.invariant: XOR is associative and self-cancelling, so every pair vanishes and the loner survives.

approaches.text: Fold the array with XOR.

problems.title: Number of 1 Bits
problems.state: Repeatedly apply n &= n-1.
problems.invariant: n & (n-1) clears exactly the lowest set bit, so the loop runs popcount times, not 32.

approaches.text: Shift and test all 32 bit positions.
Brian Kernighan's clear-lowest-set-bit.

problems.why: Iterations scale with the number of set bits rather than the word width.

problems.title: Counting Bits
problems.state: DP array indexed by number.
problems.invariant: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1) — dropping the low bit gives a smaller number already solved.

approaches.text: Kernighan popcount per number.
DP off the shifted index.

problems.why: Each answer is one addition away from an answer you already have.

problems.title: Reverse Bits
problems.state: Result accumulator, exactly 32 iterations.
problems.invariant: Shift the result left, push in n's lowest bit, shift n right — the reversal falls out by construction.

approaches.text: 32-step shift-and-push.

traps: Use the unsigned shift >>> — a signed >> smears the sign bit forever.

problems.title: Single Number II
problems.state: Two accumulators ones and twos forming a mod-3 counter.
problems.invariant: Each bit position is counted modulo 3, so bits appearing three times cancel and only the singleton's bits remain.

approaches.text: Sum each of the 32 bit positions, take mod 3.
Two-variable mod-3 state machine.

problems.why: The mod-3 counter runs bitwise-parallel across all 32 positions at once.
traps: Order matters: update ones first, then twos using the NEW ones.

problems.title: Sum of Two Integers
problems.state: a ^ b = sum without carry; (a & b) << 1 = the carry.
problems.invariant: Repeat until the carry is zero — this is a ripple-carry adder written as a loop.

approaches.text: Iterative carry propagation.

problems.title: Subsets
problems.state: Start index i + a mutable path.
problems.invariant: Every node of the recursion tree is itself a valid subset, so you record on entry rather than only at leaves.

approaches.text: Bitmask over 0 .. 2ⁿ−1.
Include/exclude recursion with an in-place path.

problems.why: Same cost, but the recursion is the shape the harder variants build on.
problems.code:
def subsets(nums):
    res, path = [], []

    def dfs(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        path.append(nums[i])           # include nums[i]
        dfs(i + 1)
        path.pop()
        dfs(i + 1)                     # exclude nums[i]

    dfs(0)
    return res

problems.title: Subsets II
problems.state: Sorted array; skip duplicates among siblings at the same depth.
problems.invariant: if (j > i && a[j] == a[j-1]) continue blocks a repeat only between siblings, never along a path.

approaches.text: Sort + sibling-level duplicate skip.

problems.why: The j > i guard is what distinguishes "same value at this level" from "same value deeper down".

problems.title: Combination Sum
problems.state: Start index i (reusable) + remaining target.
problems.invariant: Recursing with the same index allows reuse; never going below i prevents permuted duplicates.

approaches.text: Recursion passing j (not j+1) as the next start.

problems.why: dfs(j) vs dfs(j+1) is the single character that separates unbounded from 0/1 here.

problems.title: Combination Sum II
problems.state: Sorted; each element used once (dfs(j+1)) + sibling dedupe.
problems.invariant: Sorting plus the sibling-skip guard makes each multiset appear exactly once.

approaches.text: Sort + skip sibling duplicates + advance the index.

problems.why: It is Subsets II and Combination Sum composed — both guards, together.

problems.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
problems.state: Digit index + path.
problems.invariant: Depth equals the digit index, so a path of full length is automatically a complete answer.

approaches.text: Depth-indexed recursion over the keypad map.

problems.title: Generate Parentheses
problems.state: Counts open and close.
problems.invariant: Prune by open < n and close < open — every partial string stays a valid prefix, so no validity check is ever needed.

approaches.text: Generate all 2^(2n) strings and validate each.
Constrained recursion (Catalan-many leaves).

problems.why: The two counters make invalid branches unreachable rather than filtered afterwards.
problems.code:
def generate_parenthesis(n):
    res, path = [], []

    def dfs(opened, closed):
        if len(path) == 2 * n:
            res.append(''.join(path))
            return
        if opened < n:                 # can still open
            path.append('(')
            dfs(opened + 1, closed)
            path.pop()
        if closed < opened:            # can only close what is open
            path.append(')')
            dfs(opened, closed + 1)
            path.pop()

    dfs(0, 0)
    return res

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning
problems.state: Start index; try every end; recurse only on palindromic prefixes.
problems.invariant: The prefix [start, end] must be a palindrome before you recurse — that check is the pruning.

approaches.text: Backtracking with an isPalindrome guard.

problems.why: Precomputing an isPal[i][j] table turns the guard into O(1) if you need the constant factor.
problems.code:
def partition(s):
    res, path = [], []

    def dfs(start):
        if start == len(s):
            res.append(path[:])
            return
        for end in range(start + 1, len(s) + 1):
            piece = s[start:end]
            if piece == piece[::-1]:   # recurse only on palindromic prefixes
                path.append(piece)
                dfs(end)
                path.pop()

    dfs(0)
    return res

problems.title: Permutations
problems.state: In-place swap at index i (or a used[] array + path).
problems.invariant: The prefix [0, i) is fixed and every element from i onward gets its turn in slot i.

approaches.text: used[] boolean array + a path list.
In-place swap and recurse.

problems.why: The swap version needs no auxiliary array — the array itself carries the state.
problems.code:
def permute(nums):
    res = []

    def dfs(i):                        # nums[:i] is fixed
        if i == len(nums):
            res.append(nums[:])
            return
        for j in range(i, len(nums)):
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]   # choose nums[j] for slot i
            dfs(i + 1)
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]   # undo

    dfs(0)
    return res

problems.title: Permutations II
problems.state: Sorted array + used[]; skip a duplicate whose identical predecessor is currently unused.
problems.invariant: if (j > 0 && a[j] == a[j-1] && !used[j-1]) continue forces equal values to be consumed strictly left to right.

approaches.text: Sort + used[] with the predecessor-unused guard.

problems.why: Only one canonical consumption order per duplicate group is allowed, so each permutation is generated once.
traps: The swap trick from Permutations does NOT dedupe — you need sorted + used[] here.

problems.title: Valid Sudoku
problems.state: Three sets (or bitmasks): rows[9], cols[9], boxes[9].
problems.invariant: Box index is (r/3)*3 + c/3 — that formula is the only non-obvious part of the problem.

approaches.text: Single pass inserting into three sets.

problems.title: Word Search
problems.state: DFS with in-place marking (grid[r][c] = '#') restored on the way out.
problems.invariant: The marked cell cannot be reused within the current path but is freed again for every other path.

approaches.text: Grid DFS with mark-and-restore.

problems.why: Restoring on backtrack is the difference between "visited on this path" and "visited ever".

problems.title: N-Queens
problems.state: Three boolean sets — col[c], diag[r-c+n], anti[r+c].
problems.invariant: One queen per row by construction, so only the column and the two diagonal keys need checking.

approaches.text: Scan the board for conflicts before each placement.
Three O(1) conflict sets keyed by column and diagonal.

problems.why: r-c and r+c are constant along a diagonal, which turns the conflict test into an array lookup.
problems.code:
def solve_n_queens(n):
    cols, diag, anti = set(), set(), set()   # c, r - c, r + c
    board = [['.'] * n for _ in range(n)]
    res = []

    def dfs(r):
        if r == n:
            res.append([''.join(row) for row in board])
            return
        for c in range(n):
            if c in cols or r - c in diag or r + c in anti:
                continue
            cols.add(c)
            diag.add(r - c)
            anti.add(r + c)
            board[r][c] = 'Q'
            dfs(r + 1)
            cols.remove(c)
            diag.remove(r - c)
            anti.remove(r + c)
            board[r][c] = '.'

    dfs(0)
    return res

problems.title: N-Queens II
problems.state: Identical conflict sets; count instead of building boards.
problems.invariant: Same placement invariant — only the leaf action changes.

approaches.text: Same three conflict sets, incrementing a counter at depth n.

problems.why: Dropping the board construction is the whole difference, and it is where the constant factor goes.

problems.title: Climbing Stairs
problems.state: Two rolling variables.
problems.invariant: ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2) — the last step was either 1 or 2.

approaches.text: dp array of size n.
Two rolling variables.

problems.why: The recurrence reaches back only two steps, so only two values need to exist.

problems.title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
problems.state: Two rolling costs.
problems.invariant: dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]); you may start at index 0 or 1 and step past the top.

approaches.text: Two rolling variables.

problems.title: House Robber
problems.state: rob (best including i) and skip (best excluding i).
problems.invariant: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + a[i]) — adjacency is the only constraint.

approaches.text: Two rolling states.

problems.title: House Robber II
problems.state: Two independent linear runs.
problems.invariant: The first and last house are mutually exclusive, so the answer is max(rob(0..n-2), rob(1..n-1)).

approaches.text: Reduce the circle to two line problems.

problems.why: Fixing the exclusion up front removes the circularity entirely.

problems.title: Decode Ways
problems.state: Two rolling counts.
problems.invariant: dp[i] adds dp[i-1] when s[i] != '0', and dp[i-2] when s[i-1..i] lies in [10, 26].

approaches.text: Two rolling variables.

traps: '0' is only ever valid as the second digit of 10 or 20 — leading zeros kill the whole branch.

problems.title: Word Break
problems.state: dp[i] = "the prefix of length i is segmentable".
problems.invariant: dp[i] is true iff some j < i has dp[j] true and s[j..i) in the dictionary.

approaches.text: Memoised recursion over start indices.
Bottom-up DP over prefixes with a HashSet.

problems.why: Bottom-up removes the recursion and makes the memo dimension explicit.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
problems.state: Three rolling states — hold, sold, rest.
problems.invariant: sold can only come from hold; rest comes from rest or sold. The cooldown is simply the missing sold → hold edge.

approaches.text: State machine with three rolling variables.

problems.why: Drawing the three-state machine once makes the recurrence unforgettable.

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.state: Boolean dp[sum], inner loop iterated downward.
problems.invariant: dp[s] means "sum s is reachable"; the reverse inner loop guarantees each item is used at most once.

approaches.text: 2D dp[i][s] table.
1D rolling array, inner loop from S down to a[i].

problems.why: Descending order reads only previous-row values — that is exactly what makes it 0/1 and not unbounded.
traps: Ascend the inner loop and you silently solve the unbounded version instead.

problems.title: Target Sum
problems.state: Reduce to subset-sum: P = (total + target) / 2, then count subsets summing to P.
problems.invariant: Splitting into a positive set P and a negative set N with P+N = total, P−N = target makes this a counting knapsack.

approaches.text: Memoised DFS on (index, runningSum).
Algebraic reduction to a counting 0/1 knapsack.

problems.why: The reduction turns a sign-assignment search into one counting DP over sums.

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.state: dp[amount] = fewest coins; inner loop ascending.
problems.invariant: The ascending inner loop lets a coin be reused within the same row — that is the unbounded part.

approaches.text: BFS over amounts, one coin per level.
Bottom-up DP, ascending inner loop.

problems.why: Same complexity, no queue — and the loop direction is the only difference from 0/1.
problems.code:
def coin_change(coins, amount):
    INF = amount + 1
    dp = [0] + [INF] * amount          # dp[a]: fewest coins for amount a
    for c in coins:
        for a in range(c, amount + 1): # ascending: coin c can repeat
            dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] <= amount else -1

problems.title: Coin Change II
problems.state: dp[amount] = number of combinations; coin loop outside.
problems.invariant: Coin loop outer, amount loop inner counts combinations; swapping them counts permutations instead.

approaches.text: Bottom-up DP with the coin loop outermost.

problems.why: Loop order is the entire semantics here — memorise the order, not the recurrence.
traps: Swap the two loops and you count ordered sequences — a different (and wrong) answer.

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.state: dp[i][j] over prefixes of both strings.
problems.invariant: Match ⇒ 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; mismatch ⇒ max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

approaches.text: Full 2D table.
Two rolling rows.

problems.why: Each cell reads only the previous row and the cell to its left.

problems.title: Edit Distance
problems.state: dp[i][j] = min operations to turn a[0..i) into b[0..j).
problems.invariant: On mismatch the three moves are delete dp[i-1][j], insert dp[i][j-1], replace dp[i-1][j-1], each costing 1.

approaches.text: 2D table with rolling rows.

problems.why: Seeding row 0 and column 0 with i and j (pure inserts/deletes) is half the correctness.

problems.title: Interleaving String
problems.state: dp[i][j] = "a[0..i) and b[0..j) interleave to c[0..i+j)".
problems.invariant: The index into c is forced to i + j — which is exactly why the third dimension can be dropped.

approaches.text: Memoised recursion on (i, j, k).
2D DP using the k = i+j identity.

problems.why: Recognising k = i+j is what collapses a three-index problem to two.
traps: If len(a) + len(b) != len(c), return false immediately.

problems.title: Distinct Subsequences
problems.state: dp[j] = ways to form t[0..j); inner loop iterated downward.
problems.invariant: On a match you add dp[i-1][j-1]; on a mismatch you carry dp[i-1][j] forward — the source character is always skippable.

approaches.text: 1D DP over t, descending inner loop.

problems.why: Descending j is what keeps dp[j-1] on the previous row, as in 0/1 knapsack.

problems.title: Regular Expression Matching
problems.state: dp[i][j] over prefixes of s and p.
problems.invariant: For x*: either use zero copies (dp[i][j-2]) or consume one s character (dp[i-1][j] when x matches s[i-1]).

approaches.text: 2D DP over both prefixes.

problems.why: The star's two branches — zero copies vs one more copy — are the whole recurrence.
traps: Seed dp[0][j] so patterns like a*b*c* can match the empty string.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.state: tails[k] = the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1.
problems.invariant: tails is always sorted, so binary search finds where a new value belongs. Its length is the answer; its contents are not the LIS.

approaches.text: dp[i] = 1 + max over smaller earlier elements.
Patience sorting: binary search into a tails array.

problems.why: Keeping only the smallest tail per length keeps the array sorted, which is what licenses the binary search.
traps: Use lowerBound for strictly increasing, upperBound for non-decreasing.

problems.title: Unique Paths
problems.state: One rolling row.
problems.invariant: dp[j] += dp[j-1] — the left value is this row, the existing value is the row above.

approaches.text: Full 2D grid DP.
Single rolling row (or the closed form C(m+n-2, m-1)).

problems.why: Each cell reads only above and left, both of which live in one row buffer.

problems.title: Unique Paths II
problems.state: Same rolling row, with obstacles zeroed.
problems.invariant: An obstacle sets dp[j] = 0, which correctly kills every path routed through it.

approaches.text: Rolling row with obstacle zeroing.

traps: An obstacle in the first row or column zeroes everything after it — handle the seeding carefully.

problems.title: Minimum Path Sum
problems.state: Rolling row of minimum costs.
problems.invariant: dp[j] = grid[i][j] + min(above, left); the first row and column have only one predecessor.

approaches.text: Rolling row DP.

problems.title: Maximal Square
problems.state: dp[i][j] = side of the largest square whose bottom-right corner is (i, j).
problems.invariant: dp[i][j] = 1 + min(up, left, diag) — the square is limited by its weakest of three neighbours.

approaches.text: 2D table, answer = max side squared.
approaches.complexity: O(mn) / O(n) with a diagonal carry

problems.why: Anchoring at the bottom-right corner is what makes the three-neighbour minimum well defined.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
problems.state: DFS + a memo grid.
problems.invariant: Strictly increasing moves make the graph a DAG, so no visited set is needed and memo entries are final on first write.

approaches.text: Peel by out-degree (topological sort).
DFS with memoisation.

problems.why: Strict increase rules out cycles, so memoised DFS needs no cycle bookkeeping at all.

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.state: Expand around each of the 2n-1 centres.
problems.invariant: Every palindrome has a centre, and expansion stops at the first mismatch.

approaches.text: dp[i][j] table over all substrings.
Expand around centre.

problems.why: No table needed — centre expansion visits the same states in constant space.

problems.title: Palindromic Substrings
problems.state: Same centre expansion, counting each successful step.
problems.invariant: Every expansion step that still matches is one more distinct palindromic substring.

approaches.text: Expand around centre, counting.

problems.title: Burst Balloons
problems.state: dp[i][j] over the open interval (i, j); array padded with 1s at both ends.
problems.invariant: Iterate on the last balloon burst in the interval — then its neighbours are exactly the fixed boundaries i and j.

approaches.text: Backtracking over burst orders.
Interval DP on "last to burst".

problems.why: Choosing the last burst rather than the first makes the two subproblems independent.
traps: Pick the FIRST balloon to burst and the subproblems stay coupled — the DP breaks.

problems.title: Jump Game
problems.state: Single variable: the farthest reachable index.
problems.invariant: Reachability is a prefix property — if i > farthest you are stuck; otherwise extend.

approaches.text: DP over "can I reach the end from i".
One greedy reach scan.

problems.why: Only the maximum reach matters, never which index produced it.

problems.title: Jump Game II
problems.state: curEnd (end of the current level), far, jumps.
problems.invariant: This is BFS by levels — a "level" is the set of indices reachable in the same number of jumps.

approaches.text: DP for minimum jumps to each index.
Implicit level BFS with two pointers.

problems.why: Within a level only the farthest reach matters, so the whole level collapses to one number.
problems.code:
def jump(nums):
    jumps = cur_end = far = 0
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
        far = max(far, i + nums[i])
        if i == cur_end:               # end of this BFS level: must jump
            jumps += 1
            cur_end = far
    return jumps

problems.state: total surplus, running tank, candidate start.
problems.invariant: If the tank goes negative at i, then no station in [start, i] can be a valid start — so jump start to i+1.

approaches.text: Try every start index.
One pass with a reset.

problems.why: A failing prefix rules out every start inside it, not just the one you tried.
problems.code:
def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
    total = tank = start = 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        surplus = gas[i] - cost[i]
        total += surplus
        tank += surplus
        if tank < 0:                   # can't reach i+1 from start: restart there
            start, tank = i + 1, 0
    return start if total >= 0 else -1

problems.invariant: A partition can close only when i reaches the maximum last-index of every character seen so far.

count[26] signature as the key.

def rotate(matrix):
    n = len(matrix)
    for i in range(n):                 # transpose
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            matrix[i][j], matrix[j][i] = matrix[j][i], matrix[i][j]
    for row in matrix:                 # then mirror each row
        row.reverse()

problems.title: Add Two Numbers
problems.state: Dummy head + carry.
problems.invariant: Loop while either list remains OR the carry is non-zero — the trailing carry is the classic miss.

def add_two_numbers(l1, l2):
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    carry = 0
    while l1 or l2 or carry:
        total = carry + (l1.val if l1 else 0) + (l2.val if l2 else 0)
        carry, digit = divmod(total, 10)
        tail.next = ListNode(digit)
        tail = tail.next
        l1 = l1.next if l1 else None
        l2 = l2.next if l2 else None
    return dummy.next
